header.scope: Won: online membership billing only; front-desk processing at the studios is still with Global Payments, and phase two has no date.
header.tag_why: The paper sat with the controller for two weeks, and he signed four days after Tobi's session on the customer's own failed renewals; the front desk, where we couldn't show a single-screen setup, stayed with Global.

evidence.excerpt: Churn. They report member churn to the board every quarter, it had ticked up two quarters running
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: The evaluation started as a board-level churn problem, not a payments problem. Failed payments only became visible once someone split the churn number. The customer framed it as lost members; we sell it as failed-payment recovery. The size of the bucket sits in Maya's board deck, but the rep doesn't know it, so we can't size the win.
trigger.messaging: Lead M10 with the churn line the board already tracks: split your churn into cancellations and failed cards, and recover the members who never meant to leave.

decider.insight: The rep's first answer named the champion, and it rested on Maya's own claim. The controller, who signed and held the deal for two weeks, came up only under pressure. Greg was silent until we showed him his own numbers and asked about termination fees twice, so his questions were about money and exit risk. Our pitch to Maya wasn't built to answer those.
decider.messaging: Build a controller-facing version of the recovery story (recoverable revenue from their own file, plus contract term and exit cost spelled out), because the person who signs is not the person who evaluates.

evidence.excerpt: they came back with a rate review and a new terminal bundle for the front desks, on a longer contract.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: what readers do you have, do they work inside our studio software, what's the contract term, what does it cost to get out.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: My read is they were rattled, but that's my read, not hers.
evidence.label: opinion

competitor.insight: Global didn't compete on failed payments. Per Maya, it countered with rates, front-desk terminals and a longer term, and the customer's questions moved straight to hardware and exit costs. That moved the fight to the front desk, where we depend on a partner, and the front desk is exactly what Global kept. Whether the customer accepted Global's longer contract for the studios is unknown, and that matters for phase two.
competitor.messaging: When the incumbent counters with hardware and a longer term, answer with a clear view of contract term and exit cost, and don't let the conversation leave the churn problem only we addressed.

evidence.excerpt: Their file, not our average.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence. I opened with the global slide. They have studios in the US and a handful in Canada.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: when I said "unified commerce," Maya goes, "is that the readers?"
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: What landed was their own failed renewals, not a claimed uplift or an average. That cuts against M6's independent-study proof and M4's average uplift. The M1 global opener meant nothing to a customer in the US and a handful of Canadian locations. M3's term unified commerce didn't register as a concept: Maya translated it into hardware.
message.messaging: Replace the global opener and average-based proof with an offer to run the prospect's own failed-payment export, and drop the phrase unified commerce in favor of the concrete front-desk scenario.

decided.insight: The deal turned on one artifact: a spreadsheet of the customer's own recoverable renewals that the silent controller asked to keep. By the rep's own account, we were a pricing foil until then. What the spreadsheet showed in money terms, and what Greg did with it, wasn't asked, so we don't know which number moved him.
decided.messaging: Make the own-data recovery analysis a standard deliverable that ends in a spreadsheet the finance owner can take away, not a slide.

gaps.insight: M3 promises online and in-store on one platform. Here, in-store meant a partner integration the customer saw only in the partner's demo, not in their own setup, and the front desk stayed with Global. The win is half a deal, and the other half has no date and hinges on a dependency we don't control.
gaps.messaging: Stop claiming one platform for in-store where we rely on a partner integration; state which studio software is supported and show it in a live one-screen check-in-and-sale demo before claiming unified.

close.rep_takeaway: Your best move was letting Tobi run their own failed-renewals file. It's what woke up the controller who actually signed. Next time, find the person holding the paper early instead of taking the champion's word that it's her call. And report a partial win as partial: memberships are won, the front desk isn't.
